findings.title: The global compiled-pattern cache is keyed by the pattern alone, so a custom regex compiler can be silently bypassed
findings.impact: A consumer that installs a stricter or safer regex engine - typically to add a matching timeout or to reject patterns that the default engine treats as valid - can have that choice ignored for any pattern another document compiled first, so the control silently degrades to the default engine. The unbounded growth is a slow memory leak in spec-hosting processes.
findings.evidence: compilePattern stores its result with `compiledPatterns.Store(pattern, cp)` (schema_pattern.go:34) and the lookup at schema.go:2655 is `compiledPatterns.Load(schema.Pattern)`. Neither side records which compiler produced the entry, and compiledPatterns is a package-level sync.Map (schema.go:46) shared by every document, every Loader and every request in the process. Two consequences follow from the same line: a matcher compiled by the default Go engine is returned to a caller that asked for a different one through SetSchemaRegexCompiler or openapi3filter Options.RegexCompiler, whenever any earlier document used the same pattern string; and the map has no bound and no eviction, so a long-lived process that loads many documents accumulates one entry per distinct pattern for its lifetime. findings.title: Legacy Router.AddRoute stores the wrong value type, so FindRoute can return a nil route with a nil error
findings.impact: A route registered through the exported AddRoute API is silently destroyed and, from then on, every request matching it makes the validating middleware dereference a nil pointer - a panic per request on that endpoint rather than a validation result. The contract violation is the deeper problem: FindRoute promises that a nil error implies a usable route, and here it does not.
findings.evidence: NewRouter stores a *routers.Route in each trie node (router.go:66-71). AddRoute, an exported method, stores the *Router itself instead: `return router.node().Add(method+" "+path, router, nil)` (:95). FindRoute reads nodes back with a type assertion, `route, _ = node.Value.(*routers.Route)` (:143), which fails for such a node and leaves route nil. Execution then enters the `if route == nil` block at :145; when the path is also a declared path with that method - which is exactly the case after AddRoute overwrites a node NewRouter had already populated - neither early return fires, and the function reaches `return route, pathParams, nil` at :163 with route nil and err nil. Every documented caller then dereferences it: openapi3filter/middleware.go:122-133 treats a nil error as success and passes the nil Route into ValidateRequest, whose first statements are `route := input.Route; operation :

findings.title: CI job exports GITHUB_TOKEN to every step and declares no permissions block while building untrusted pull-request code
findings.impact: Code proposed by a contributor runs in the same process environment as the workflow token. For pull requests opened from forks GitHub downgrades that token to read-only, which bounds the damage to reading; for branches inside the repository and for push events the token carries the repository default, and if that default is the permissive read-write set the executed test code can use it against the repository's own API surface.
findings.evidence: .github/workflows/go.yml has no `permissions:` key at workflow or job level, so the job receives whatever the repository or organisation sets as the default GITHUB_TOKEN scope. Line 8-13 puts the token in the job-level env block - `GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` - which places it in the environment of every subsequent step, including the ones that execute contributor-supplied code checked out at line 36: `go generate ./...` (:38), `./maps.sh` (:41), `./docs.sh` (:44) and `go test ./...` (:56 and following). The trigger is `pull_request` (:3), not pull_request_target, which is the safe choice and is why this is rated as it is rather than higher.

findings.title: Query-string array index sizes an unbounded slice allocation in the deepObject decoder
findings.impact: An unauthenticated client - authenticated only where the operation declares a security requirement - drives the server process into memory exhaustion and OOM termination with a single short request, and can repeat it. This is an availability compromise of the whole host process, not of one request: the allocation happens in the decoder, before any schema constraint is evaluated.
findings.evidence: Source-to-sink, all inside code in scope. Source: urlValuesDecoder.DecodeObject, style deepObject (req_resp_decoder.go:661-686) walks every query parameter name, extracts the bracketed segments with `\[(.*?)\]` and joins them into a props key; the last segment of `?filter[ids][N]=x` becomes the map key "N", entirely attacker-chosen. makeObject (:911) splits that key and deepSet (:899) builds mobj = {"ids": {"N": "x"}}. buildResObj (:965) sees an array-typed property, takes the map branch at :976-981 and calls sliceMapToSlice (:936). There, every key is parsed with strconv.Atoi (:941) - which accepts any int64 - and the maximum is taken at :947-951 with no comparison against anything the client does not control. findings.title: CI runs third-party actions pinned only by tag and executes four Go tools resolved at @latest
findings.impact: Compromise of any of those upstream repositories, of a maintainer account able to move a tag, or of a module publishing account, results in attacker-chosen code executing inside this project's CI with the workflow token in its environment (see F-006) and, for the modernize step, with permission to modify the checked-out source before the test and diff steps run.
findings.evidence: Mutable references executed by the pipeline: go.yml uses actions/setup-go@v6 (:27), actions/cache@v3 (:31) and actions/checkout@v6 (:36 and :143); shellcheck.yml uses actions/checkout@v2 (:11) and the third-party action ludeeus/action-shellcheck@1.1.0 (:13). A Git tag is movable, so none of these identifies an immutable artifact. Worse, four steps fetch and execute code resolved at build time: `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/modernize/cmd/modernize@latest -test -diff -fix ...` (:62, and note it runs with -fix, i.e. it is allowed to rewrite the tree), `go run golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis/passes/nilness/cmd/nilness@latest ./...` (:87), `go install github.com/incu6us/goimports-reviser/v3@latest` (:148) and `go run -a github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/cmd/validate@latest ...` (:129). @latest is resolved against the module proxy at run time, so the code executed on any given day i

findings.title: An AWS access key ID is tracked in a vendored third-party spec fixture
findings.impact: None reachable. An AWS access key ID is an identifier rather than a secret; the matching secret access key is not present, and the signature it accompanies expired 3600 seconds after 2017-07-28. What it grants is the identity of an AWS account belonging to a third party, which is recorded here so that a reader does not have to re-derive it and so that an automated secret scanner's alert on this repository has a known answer.
findings.evidence: A scan of all 1,667 non-.git files for the high-precision credential formats (the GitHub, Slack, GitLab and Anthropic token prefixes, the AWS access-key-identifier prefix and the PEM private-key header) returns exactly one hit: line 29766 of openapi3/testdata/oai_v3_stoplight.json contains a documentation example of an AWS pre-signed S3 URL whose X-Amz-Credential parameter carries an AWS access key ID, [REDACTED:secret], alongside X-Amz-Date=20170728T223936Z, X-Amz-Expires=3600 and a truncated X-Amz-Signature. openapi3/issue594_test.go:13 records the file's provenance: it is a verbatim copy of sendgrid/sendgrid-oai's oai_v3_stoplight.json, i.e. a third party's public API document, not material authored here. No other credential format from that set appears anywhere in the tree.

findings.title: Request bodies are buffered and decoded with no size limit, and the pre-authentication read has none either
findings.impact: Concurrent clients hold an unbounded and amplified amount of server memory. Because the read in validateSecurityRequirement precedes authentication, an operation that requires credentials still buffers the attacker's body in full before rejecting them, so the cost cannot be shed by the auth layer the library itself invokes.
findings.evidence: validate_request.go:271 - `data, err = io.ReadAll(req.Body)` with no wrapping MaxBytesReader and no configurable cap; the same unbounded read appears at :448 inside validateSecurityRequirement, which runs before the AuthenticationFunc is called, so the whole body is resident in memory before the request is known to be authenticated. The buffered bytes are then handed to decodeBody (:324) and, for the default JSON media types, to JSONBodyDecoder (req_resp_decoder.go:1361) which decodes into an `any` tree: a body of repeated small JSON scalars expands into interface headers, json.Number strings and map buckets many times the size of the wire representation, so the peak is a multiple of the bytes sent. openapi3filter/options.go declares no limit of any kind, and grep over the tree finds no MaxBytesReader, no LimitReader and no Max*Size knob in the request path. findings.title: Legacy router panics on any request whose HTTP method is not one of the nine standard ones
findings.impact: Any client can crash the request goroutine with `curl -X PROPFIND https://host/<declared-path>`. Under net/http the panic is recovered per connection, so the effect is a 500, a dropped connection and a full stack trace written to the server error log on every attempt - a cheap log-flooding and internal-path-disclosure primitive. Where the router is driven outside an http.Server's recover (a worker goroutine, a Lambda-style handler, a gateway with its own dispatch loop), the same request terminates the process.
findings.evidence: openapi3/path_item.go:153-176 - GetOperation switches on the nine methods of net/http and its default branch is `panic(fmt.Errorf("unsupported HTTP method %q", method))`. routers/legacy/router.go:109 takes `method := req.Method` verbatim from the request; net/http accepts any RFC 7230 token as a method, so this is an arbitrary attacker-supplied string. Line 141 asks the pathpattern trie for `method + " " + remainingPath`; the trie was built in NewRouter (:66-71) only from the methods returned by PathItem.Operations(), which are the nine standard ones upper-cased, so an unknown method never matches and node is nil. Line 148 then falls back to an exact map lookup, `doc.Paths.Value(remainingPath)`, which succeeds for any literal declared path such as /health or /users, and line 150 calls pathItem.GetOperation(method) with the attacker's token, reaching the panic. findings.title: Enabling external $ref resolution grants a document arbitrary local file reads and arbitrary outbound HTTP with no allowlist or timeout
findings.impact: A service or tool that resolves external references in documents it did not author lets the document's author read any file the process can read and reach any host the process can reach - the classic SSRF pivot to a cloud metadata endpoint or an internal service - with the fetched bytes ending up inside the parsed document and therefore inside whatever the tool prints, renders or stores.
findings.evidence: One boolean, Loader.IsExternalRefsAllowed, gates two very different capabilities. When it is set, resolvePath (loader.go:307-317, the absolute-path branch at :310) returns an absolute $ref path unchanged - `if filepath.IsAbs(componentPath.Path) { return componentPath }` - and otherwise joins it with path.Join against the document's directory, which resolves `../` upward without any containment check; ReadFromFile (loader_uri_reader.go:78-84) then calls os.ReadFile on the result, so `$ref: "/etc/passwd"` and `$ref: "../../../../etc/shadow"` are both honoured. The same flag admits ReadFromHTTP (:51-69), which issues a GET to any scheme/host in the $ref through http.DefaultClient - a client with no timeout and no host, scheme or address restriction - so `$ref: "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/"` is fetched, its body is unmarshalled into the document, and a hostile or slow host can a

findings.title: String validation dereferences a nil matcher when a pattern fails to compile and MultiError is enabled
findings.impact: A panic during request validation instead of a validation error: a 500 and a logged stack trace under net/http, process termination where no recover is in place.
findings.evidence: schema.go:2655-2680: the cache is consulted, and on a miss compilePattern is called. On a compile failure the error is returned only when multiError is off (`if !settings.multiError { return err }`); with multiError on the error is appended to the accumulator and execution continues to :2666, `if !cp.MatchString(value)`. compilePattern (schema_pattern.go:19-35) assigns the result of regexp.Compile straight into the RegexMatcher interface, so a failure leaves cp holding a typed nil *regexp.Regexp - an interface that is not nil and whose method call dereferences a nil receiver - and a custom RegexCompilerFunc returning (nil, err) leaves cp as an untyped nil interface. Either way :2666 panics rather than reporting the error it just recorded.

findings.title: ValidationHandler silently replaces a missing AuthenticationFunc with one that approves everything
findings.impact: A service that mounts ValidationHandler and relies on it to enforce the security requirements declared in its own OpenAPI document enforces nothing: every request is treated as satisfying every declared scheme, and the failure is silent at construction time and at request time. Whether an unauthenticated caller actually reaches protected functionality then depends on whether the wrapped handler performs its own check.
findings.evidence: The core validator fails closed: validate_request.go:431-433 returns ErrAuthenticationServiceMissing when Options.AuthenticationFunc is nil, so a consumer who forgets to supply one gets an error on every request. ValidationHandler.Load reverses that at validation_handler.go:47-49 - `if h.AuthenticationFunc == nil { h.AuthenticationFunc = NoopAuthenticationFunc }` - and NoopAuthenticationFunc (:18) is `return nil`, i.e. every security scheme of every operation is declared satisfied. That value is then handed straight to Options.AuthenticationFunc at validation_handler.go:92. Load returns no error and logs nothing. The struct field carries no warning comment, and the README contains no occurrence of 'AuthenticationFunc', 'security' or 'Noop' at all, so nothing in the repository tells the caller that the default is permissive.

findings.title: ZipFileBodyDecoder appends the whole read buffer regardless of how many bytes were read
findings.impact: For any consumer that registers this decoder, schema validation is performed against corrupted content - trailing garbage can make a value that should fail minLength/pattern/format checks pass, or vice versa - and the decoded string grows to a multiple of the archive's real size, adding an unnecessary memory factor on top of the documented decompression risk.
findings.evidence: The read loop at req_resp_decoder.go:1634-1646 captures the byte count as `n, err := rc.Read(buffer)` and then, at :1639, appends the entire fixed 256-byte buffer: `if 0 < n { content = append(content, buffer...) }`. The count n is never used. Every short read therefore contributes 256 bytes to the decoded value: the tail of the previous read is re-emitted as if it were file content, and the decoded string is longer than the archive's actual contents. The value produced here is what ValidateRequestBody then hands to Schema.VisitJSON, so the bytes that are validated are not the bytes that were uploaded. The same function carries its own warning about zip bombs in the doc comment at :1608-1609; that part is disclosed, this part is not.

findings.title: deepObject decoding compiles two regular expressions per query parameter on every request
findings.impact: A single request carrying a large number of distinct query parameters converts a small amount of network traffic into a disproportionate amount of server CPU. It is an amplification factor on an existing surface rather than a new capability, which is why it is rated low.
findings.evidence: req_resp_decoder.go:663-686 iterates over every key of url.Values and, inside the loop body, calls regexp.MustCompile twice: at :665 for `^<param>\[` and at :669 for `\[(.*?)\]`. Neither pattern depends on the loop variable in a way that prevents hoisting - the first depends only on the parameter name, the second on nothing at all - yet both are recompiled for each of the N query parameters, on each request, for each deepObject parameter the operation declares. Compilation, not matching, dominates: the work is O(N) regexp compilations where N is chosen by the client and is bounded only by the server's MaxHeaderBytes.

findings.title: Request decoder dereferences five schema pointers that the document is allowed to omit
findings.impact: A client turns a well-formed request into a runtime panic. Under net/http the panic is recovered, so the observable result is a 500 with a stack trace in the log instead of the 400 the caller should have received; outside an http.Server's recover it terminates the process. In the urlencoded case the panic is unconditional for that operation, so the endpoint is unusable for every client, not only the attacker.
findings.evidence:
The decoder assumes schema fields that the document validator treats as optional, in five places, each reachable by a request.
(a) A parameter declared with `content:` but no `schema:` is accepted by openapi3/media_type.go:125 - `if schema := mediaType.Schema; schema != nil` - so nothing rejects it. req_resp_decoder.go:195 then does `outSchema = mt.Schema.Value` with no guard, and decodeContentParameter only reaches it once the client actually supplies the parameter (:145-149 returns early when it is absent). This one is version-independent: `content: {application/json: {}}` on any 3.x document is enough.
(b)-(e) openapi3/schema.go:1690 makes `items` optional whenever jsonSchema2020ValidationEnabled is set, and openapi3/openapi3.go:268-271 with validation_options.go:39-42 sets it automatically for every document at 3.1 or later, so `type: array` with no `items` passes doc.Validate(). Fou

advisories_to_match.summary: kin-openapi has uncontrolled resource consumption in openapi3filter deepObject query parameter decoding
advisories_to_match.description:
### Summary

An uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability in `openapi3filter` lets any unauthenticated client force multi-gigabyte heap allocation with a single, tiny HTTP request. When a spec declares a `deepObject`-style query parameter whose schema contains an array (a normal, documented pattern), the decoder reconstructs the array by reading the **largest attacker-supplied index** and allocating one slot for every position from `0` up to that index — *before* schema validation (including `maxItems`) ever runs. A request as small as 24 bytes (`?param[items][50000000]=x`) drives heap allocation to **~6.1 GiB**, reliably triggering an OOM kill / restart loop on memory-constrained services.

### Details

The OpenAPI `style: deepObject` serialization lets clients express arrays in the query string using bracket notation, e.g. `param[items][0]=a&param[items][1]=b`. The decoder first collects these into an intermediate `map[string]any` keyed by the string of the index, then converts that sparse map into a real `[]any` in [`sliceMapToSlice`](https://github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/blob/master/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go#L936):
